thread.title: Apple Nearing Important Point - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)

author: Bill Maurer
title: Apple Nearing Important Point - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)
text:
It's not been a pretty couple of months for shares of Apple ( AAPL ). Between the US/China trade war and concerns over iPhone sales, shares have dropped almost 30% from their all-time high as seen below. With market cap losses in the hundreds of billions piling up, shares of the company are approaching a critical point in the Apple story.
( Source: Yahoo! Finance)
Last Friday, Apple shares broke below $170, falling below their late November low. While I warned investors not to buy the bounce , I'd rather not take credit for my prediction that shares would go lower, given what we've seen in the overall market. We continue to see more analysts worrying about the name, with a note last week from UBS talking about weak iPhone purchase intent . Also, one of the biggest Apple bulls at Morgan Stanley cut her price target on the name based on weak China sales .
As all dividend investors know, a falling stock means that the name's dividend yield is rising. Apple currently pays a $2.92 annual dividend, which as you can see from the chart below, currently means a yield of more than 1.70%. In the last six months, the fall in shares means a rise in that daily closing yield of about 50 basis points from the low under 1.30%. With such a large drop in the stock, I am no longer convinced in my late August stance that the dividend should be raised again ahead of the expected raise next Spring.
So what's the big deal about a rising dividend yield? Well, the key point I'm referring to happens to be associated with the company's massive buyback. In recent quarters, management has spent tens of billions to repurchase shares. With the sharp rise in the stock, the average price paid has soared, well over $200 in some cases in the most recent quarter. The pullback will certainly help with that, because every billion goes a lot further with a near 30% decline.
Apple's buyback strategy has changed over the past year thanks to the change in US tax laws. The company repatriated a large foreign cash balance, so it is no longer taking out debt to facilitate the buyback. However, there is a cost to buying back shares, because that cash is reinvested by the company, and thus Apple is losing out on interest expenses. Here's what was said in the 10-K filing about this situation:
The weighted-average interest rate earned by the Company on its cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities was 2.16%, 1.99% and 1.73% in 2018, 2017 and 2016, respectively.
In the fiscal year ending September 2018, Apple averaged 2.16% on what we refer to as its cash pile. That of course is before taxes, which for the quarter we are currently in are projected to be 16.5% before discrete items. Assuming no change in the interest rate generated, and using that tax rate, that would mean that the post-tax yield is just around 1.80%. Gee, Apple's dividend yield is close to that point, as I've showed above, and I'm not even including the potential dividend raise next Spring that would increase dividend payments for the future 12-month period.
Why is this so important? Well, we don't know what the actual break even value actually is, because we don't know exactly what Apple's interest rate is and the true tax rate on that income gained. Only a handful of Apple employees or executives know the actual math here. However, for this argument, let's just assume Apple's dividend yield hits that point. Then, it means that when Apple buys back shares, it saves more on dividend payments than it generates in net interest income. Before you ask, yes, Apple still has to spend money to repurchase shares.
Think about this in more relative terms. Go back a few months, when Apple had a dividend yield of 1.30% and let's say its post-tax interest yield was 1.80%. That means that for every $1 billion worth of share repurchases, it was saving $13 million on dividend payments, but losing $18 million of net interest income (which goes into operating cash flow). That gap has certainly narrowed now, and we could almost be to the point where there is a cash flow "savings" generated by buying back stock. The potential savings can really add up when we are talking about repurchases that are running around $20 billion per quarter currently.
In the end, Apple shares are approaching a critical level. With the fall in the stock sending the dividend yield to its highest point in several months, we are almost to the point where the buyback becomes cash flow positive in a sense. While we don't know what the exact number is, we do know at a minimum that the gap has narrowed meaning the company's savings on dividend payments has increased to where it almost matches net interest income generated after taxes. By not losing as much cash flow in this process, the cash balance stays higher allowing for more capital returns in the future.
